007d6f6b-4f84-5cd4-97d4-b1637e409355.name: Emigrant family
007d6f6b-4f84-5cd4-97d4-b1637e409355.holder: Population Exchange Museum (The Foundation of Lausanne Treaty Emigrants)
007d6f6b-4f84-5cd4-97d4-b1637e409355.description2: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. This photo belongs to a Turkish family who migrated from Crete to Turkey in 1925.

00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.name: Constitution of the Slav-Macedonian Scientific and Literary Society in Saint Petersburg
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.holder: University of St. Cyril and Methodius - Publisher
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.archival: Documents on the Struggle of the Macedonian People for Independence and a Nation-State, Vol. I, Skopje, 1985
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.description2: The Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society was established in St. Petersburg on 16 December 1903, acting under the patronage of the St. Petersburg Slav Charitable Society. Its founders were Krste Petkov Misirkov (1874–1926) and Dimitija Chupovski, who worked actively on the recognition of Macedonian as distinct Slavic language and the opening of native-language schools for children in Macedonia. The Society, also known as the Macedonian Colony in St. Petersburg, gathered many distinguished Macedonian writers, poets and publicists. Its extensive scientific and literary activities have brought about explicit formulation of the Macedonian national program. The Society largely contributed to issuing a periodical publication in Macedonian and Russian language called “Makedonski Golos” (“Macedonian Voice"). It played an important role in the national awakening of Macedonians and bringing forth the issue of the Macedonian autonomy in the international community.

00dac457-85a0-5a63-aebd-676267b9816c.name: Société des Fermes Françaises de Tunisie
00dac457-85a0-5a63-aebd-676267b9816c.description2: French agriculture in Tunisia came about either through the establishment of large properties by private initiatives, or the arrangement of settlers by the public authorities. This is a text from the "first phase" - one of the "companies" (of "French farms") had purchased a large plot of land, and employed a number of (largely Arab and Italian) workers to cultivate it. It aims to publicise the company and make it attractive to both prospective immigrants to tunisia, and attract funds.

01425452-ab97-5882-bfb1-7f4f896ba157.name: Omar Pasha (1806–1871)
01425452-ab97-5882-bfb1-7f4f896ba157.keywords: Omar Pasha; Croatia; Bosnia; Ottoman empire; Herzegovina
01425452-ab97-5882-bfb1-7f4f896ba157.description2: Portrait of Omar Pasha. He was born in Croatia in 1806 near the Turkish-Hungarian border. In 1828 he deserted from the Austrian army and joined the Ottoman administration in Bosnia. After a long career in the Ottoman army, he became the military governor of Bucharest and commanded the Ottoman forces at the siege of Sevastopol in Crimea. In 1862 he suppressed an uprising in Herzogovina and led a victorious campaign against Montenegro. In 1868 he became War Minister and died in 1871 in Istanbul.

01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.name: Cup and a stand
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.keywords: Political and diplomatic engagement; cup; stand; metalwork; domestic vessels
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.description2: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878-1940) was a distinguished Macedonian intellectual who lived and worked in Russia. Being the President of the Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society in St. Petersburg, he contributed to the publishing of historical memorandums and other official acts that presented the national ideology and objectives for unity and liberation of Macedonia. He also published numerous articles drawing attention to the partitioning of Macedonia after the Balkan Wars. In his struggle for preserving the integrity of Macedonia he wrote various memoranda to governments of western countries on many occasions.

03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.name: Construction Site at Shellal
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.author: Patrizia Pampana
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.archival: “Bollettino della Società geografica”, serie IV, 1901, vol. II, n. 6, p. 548
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.second_name: Egyptian and migrant labourers working on the construction of the first dam on the Nile
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.description2: In 1900, Count Giulio d’Aspremont, an Italian diplomat, visited the construction site of the first dam across the Nile (today known as the Aswan Low Dam or Old Aswan Dam). He took several pictures of the works and of the monuments on the island of Philae that were going to be submerged by the water. He published some of them on the *Bulletin of the Italian Geographical Society*, where he wrote that up to 2,000 Italian workers were employed in the works (as stone-cutters, miners and masons), out of a total labour force of about 10,000 or 12,000; an Italian village had sprung up on the Nile banks, with modest little houses, trattorias and shops.

036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.name: An Italian cartoon in support of Ahmad Urabi's movement against foreign control of Egypt's finances
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.author: Giulia Barrera
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.description2:
Ahmad Urabi was an Egyptian colonel of peasant origins who led a revolt in 1879-1882 aimed at eliminating foreign control of Egyptian finances and establishing constitutional limits to the Khedive’s authority. John Bull is a recognized national personification of the United Kingdom.  
Caption: “Be careful, merchant! Despite your cannons, your ships and your money, I will be able to teach you that in places where true love for one’s country flourishes, people can make heroic miracles in order to defend their homeland!”  
Part of the Italian public opinion sided with the Egyptians, against the British, since it likened Egyptian struggle with Italian struggle for national unification and self-determination. Ironically, however, in 1882 Italy occupied Massawa, on the Red Sea, and started its own colonial expansion.
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.holding_institution_org: Biblioteca di Storia Moderna e Contemporanea

06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.name: Painting of Ahmed Pacha Bey
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.holder: Musée d’Histoire Moderne et Contemporaine de Kassar Saïd
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.keywords: Oil on canvas; Ahmed Pacha Bey; Charles Gleyre
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.materials: Canvas, wood, coloured pigments, gold leaf
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.description2: This oil on canvas portrait by the Swiss artist Charles Gleyre (1806–1874) depicts Ahmed Pacha Bey, the ruling prince of Tunisia at the time (1837–1855). He is dressed in official uniform, with red trousers with a gold strip and a black overcoat with gold epaulets, and is wearing the *muchir*'s insignia round his neck, and the Ordre du Sang, the Nichan al-Dam, and the Grand Croix de la Légion d'Honneur medals on the left of his chest. His torso his divided in two by a shimmering red sash of honour, his black and gold sword hangs off his belt on the left-hand side, and he is wearing a red chechia on his head. This painting is evidence of an active diplomatic relationship between the Palais du Bardo and the European chancelleries.

069fe14a-0c18-5f5b-a028-0bc56e4c4758.name: *Passports that French ships were obliged to carry in order to be allowed to practice privateering*
069fe14a-0c18-5f5b-a028-0bc56e4c4758.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
069fe14a-0c18-5f5b-a028-0bc56e4c4758.description2: This document is written in both Arabic and French. Bearing the sovereign's seal and signature, it guaranteed its bearer full safety for their persons and goods.

0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.name: Balkan immigrants village at Sivrihisar
0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; History of Ottoman Empire; Balkan wars; migrations
0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.description2: The civilian population living in the Balkans was forced to migrate to Anatolia due to the Balkan Wars at the end of the 18th century: the 1821 Mora rebellion, the 1856 Crimean war, the 1864 Russian-Caucasian war, the 1877-1878 Ottoman-Russian War, the 1896-97 Crete Rebellion, the 1912-13 Balkan Wars, World War I from 1914 to 1918 and the 1919-22 Greek-Turkish War. These wars resulted in mass migrations. The Ottoman Empire lost almost all its European territories west of the River Maritsa, drawing present day Turkey's western border. A large influx of Turks started to flee into the Ottoman heartland as a result of the lost lands. By 1914, the remaining core region of the Ottoman Empire had experienced a population increase of around 2.5 million because of the flood of immigration from the Balkans.

0b61c9ae-ef04-5d1e-af0b-b7e4ab248173.name: Type-writing machine
0b61c9ae-ef04-5d1e-af0b-b7e4ab248173.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
0b61c9ae-ef04-5d1e-af0b-b7e4ab248173.description2: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878-1940) was born in Papradishte near Veles, R. Macedonia in 1878. He lived in Krushevo and acquired his education in Belgrade and St. Petersburg. He was a renowned Macedonian lexicographer, textbook writer and philologist who prepared the modern grammar of Macedonian language. Chupovski also worked out the first Macedonian-Russian dictionary.

0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.name: Misrata [Libya]. In the Home of Gabrielli, Agent of the Society of Maritime Services [Società dei servizi marittimi]
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.author: Patrizia Pampana, Giulia Barrera
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.third_name: *Misràta. In casa di Gabrielli, agente della Società dei servizi marittimi*
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.description2:
In 19th and early 20th century Africa, the nature of the relations between European men and African women varied dramatically according to the different power relations between the partners. In colonial situations, the legal subordination of the colonised people put African women in particularly weak positions vis-à-vis European men, generally resulting in very exploitative relationships. In countries that were not under European rule, more balanced relationships could develop.  
This picture shows a mixed family in Libya before the onset of Italian colonialism. The setting of the picture suggests that the Libyan woman enjoyed respect and status within the family: the woman and her children are sitting on chairs, surrounded by persons who appear to be domestic servants, and the Italian man is standing behind her, looking at their children.

0b914ea4-3750-5949-ba83-6be97904425d.name: The fundamental pact
0b914ea4-3750-5949-ba83-6be97904425d.author: Bechir Yazidi
0b914ea4-3750-5949-ba83-6be97904425d.description2: This foundational text was drawn up by Mohamed Bey of the Husainid dynasty (1855–1859) under the pressure of the French and English consuls. They had the aim of either adopting or adapting the reforms introduced in Istanbul which required them to provide non-Muslim subjects with semi-secular services, such as the establishment of mixed tribunals avoiding the strict application of the Quran, and also ensured free trade for France and England.

0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.name: The Italian Politeama Rossini theatre in Tunis, inaugurated in 1903
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.author: Giulia Barrera
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 67
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.description2:
The Politeama Rossini was built by the construction company of Giuseppe Di Vittorio (a Sicilian who had migrated to Tunisia in 1882); the architect was a Mr. Baron. It could house an audience of 2,500.  
The first Italian theatre in Tunis was the “Teatro Tapia” founded in 1826. Other Italian theatres (such as the “Teatro Italiano” and the “Teatro Paradiso”) and concert halls (“Gran Teatro”, “Teatro Cohen”, etc.) were created in Tunis the following decades.

0f212b46-5c94-5a3d-875d-f50778a5c111.name: Request to the Bey of Tunis by Tunisian merchants in Istanbul
0f212b46-5c94-5a3d-875d-f50778a5c111.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
0f212b46-5c94-5a3d-875d-f50778a5c111.description2: This petition from the Jerbian merchants in Istanbul to the Bey of Tunis protests the behaviour of a Tunisian Jewish merchant.

0fbf5343-64ee-545a-b2c8-56f70b18ca50.name: Samovar
0fbf5343-64ee-545a-b2c8-56f70b18ca50.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities
0fbf5343-64ee-545a-b2c8-56f70b18ca50.keywords: Russia; Eastern and Southern Europe; Middle East; metal container; tea drinking; domestic vessels
0fbf5343-64ee-545a-b2c8-56f70b18ca50.description2: Samovars are very common in Russia, Eastern Europe and in the Middle East. The samovar is a highly decorated metal container with a tap at the bottom and a pipe that runs vertically through it. By filling the pipe with coals, it will heat the water inside the container. A teapot kept on the top of the pipe will brew a strong concentration of tea that will be served after adding boiled water to it from the container. Samovars were brought to Jordan by various north Caucasian peoples, referred to as Circassians, who immigrated to the region during the last quarter of the 19th century.

11ee08c6-3f50-5b88-b216-58be546fc86a.name: *Antonis Benakis at the Sporting Club in Alexandria*
11ee08c6-3f50-5b88-b216-58be546fc86a.author: Maria Dimitriadou
11ee08c6-3f50-5b88-b216-58be546fc86a.description2: A black and white photos from a photo album showing snapshots of a polo game at Alexandria Sporting Club and naming Antoni Benakis as the leading rider. Phototographer unknown.

16145c6c-e484-5568-ab55-c93317ec5964.name: Carol I, King of Romania (1839–1914) / Karl von Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen
16145c6c-e484-5568-ab55-c93317ec5964.keywords: Carol I, King of Romania; Karl von Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen
16145c6c-e484-5568-ab55-c93317ec5964.description2: Portrait of Carol I, King of Romania (1839–1914) in uniform with Karl von Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. He was elected Prince of Romania on the recommendation of Napoleon III in 1866. In 1881, after achieving formal independence from the Ottoman Empire, Carol declared himself King of Romania.

16fa95b3-e587-5dfb-983e-0384c05f1b3e.keywords: Italians in Egypt; Egyptian society; cosmopolitan cities; foreign communities in Egypt; industrialists; workers; craftsmen; trade; commerce; craftmanship; Italians in Alexandria; city; urban space; migration; book
16fa95b3-e587-5dfb-983e-0384c05f1b3e.third_name: L.A. Balboni, *Gli Italiani nella Civiltà Egiziana del Secolo XIX°*, Alessandria d'Egitto, 1906: frontespizio
16fa95b3-e587-5dfb-983e-0384c05f1b3e.description2: The work in three volumes, exalts the importance of the Italian settlement in Alexandria, and represents one of the most consistent literary evidence of cultural and commercial relations, as well as administrative and building activities, started by the Italian state before 1911.

183b1889-44b1-5781-a76f-71957bab4067.name: Muhammad ‘Ali Pasha (1769–1849)
183b1889-44b1-5781-a76f-71957bab4067.description2: Portrait of Muhammad 'Ali Pasha. Although born in Greece, he was the founder of modern Egypt. From Albanian origin, he came to Egypt as an Ottoman officer and began the modernisation of the Egyptian state.

19a79dbf-5845-53ed-a137-ee4c74fd1299.name: Inkpot and blotter
19a79dbf-5845-53ed-a137-ee4c74fd1299.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
19a79dbf-5845-53ed-a137-ee4c74fd1299.description2: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878-1940) devoted his life to raising the awareness of Macedonians about their national identity. He worked actively on the recognition of Macedonian as distinct Slavic language and prepared the grammar of the modern Macedonian language. He also contributed to opening schools for children in Macedonia to learn in their native language.

19adb7d5-92bf-5c8a-8b63-f8d677d0e713.name: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro (1871–1939)
19adb7d5-92bf-5c8a-8b63-f8d677d0e713.keywords: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro; Jugoslavia; Vienna; Austria
19adb7d5-92bf-5c8a-8b63-f8d677d0e713.description2: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro (1871–1939) was the eldest son of King Nicola I of Montenegro. He was married to Princess Jutta von Mecklenburg-Strelitz and had to leave Montenegro after it was integrated in the kingdom of Yugoslavia after WWI. He died in 1937 in Vienna, Austria – in exile.

1c267ea2-0ed8-59a8-a801-5398707285eb.name: Balkans, exiled civilians on the move
1c267ea2-0ed8-59a8-a801-5398707285eb.description2: The First Balkan War (1912–1913) saw the Ottoman Empire at war with Serbia, Bulgaria and Greece. The violent nature of the conflict caused many populations to be displaced.

1c651cdc-3180-5289-952f-daeae5e69f65.name: Emigrants who immigrated to America
1c651cdc-3180-5289-952f-daeae5e69f65.holder: Population Exchange Museum (The Foundation of Lausanne Treaty Emigrants)
1c651cdc-3180-5289-952f-daeae5e69f65.description2: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. This photo depicts some Muslim migrants who immigrated to America.

1e12d773-b67f-5c74-86a0-52e25a1cd507.name: *Précis Historique de la Traite des Noirs et de l'Esclavage Colonial*
1e12d773-b67f-5c74-86a0-52e25a1cd507.description2: Joseph Elzéar Morénas (1776–1830) was born to a wealthy family of merchants. Following an early trip to India, Morénas became specialised in botany and developed a love of languages, which even led him to write a Hindi dictionary. When he was sent to Senegal in 1818 he was horrified by what he saw of the slave trade, and so asked to be repatriated. After a sojourn in Haiti, he began working on research in the agricultural sciences, all the while denouncing the "slave trade". His two petitions, "*Pétition contre la traite des noirs*" (1820 and 1821), which he presented to the Chamber of Deputies, created many problems for him. He therefore began working on a *Précis Historique de la Traite des Noirs et de l'Esclavage Colonial* instead, which was published in 1828. He died in Russia, where the Tsar encouraged the continuation of his agronomical work. This title page points to his relationship with and support for Cyril Bissette, a Martinician accused of having written De la Situation des Gens de Couleur Libres aux Antilles Françaises, who was banished by the royal court along with his so-called accomplices (Fabien and Volny).

1e88ab3a-3f62-5a22-b9a2-264a8573788d.name: Two pistols
1e88ab3a-3f62-5a22-b9a2-264a8573788d.type: Military object; metalwork; firearms; arms and armour
1e88ab3a-3f62-5a22-b9a2-264a8573788d.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
1e88ab3a-3f62-5a22-b9a2-264a8573788d.keywords: Military object; Metalwork; Steel; Arms; armour; Pistol
1e88ab3a-3f62-5a22-b9a2-264a8573788d.description2: These Turkish flintlock pistols were used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. These pistols are an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. They were commonly known as "knee pistols", as they were fired from horseback by placing the butt of the pistol against the rider's knee. Both have a typical blunderbuss style stock with a beautifully shaped butt stock, a wooden forend and a round barrel. They are made of wood and cast steel.

2014af0a-f0bc-59a2-9a32-22eb77035668.name: Ferdinand I, Czar of Bulgaria (1861–1948)
2014af0a-f0bc-59a2-9a32-22eb77035668.keywords: Ferdinand I, Czar of Bulgaria; Sachsen-Coburg and Gotha
2014af0a-f0bc-59a2-9a32-22eb77035668.description2: Portrait of Ferdinand I (1861–1948) as Duke of Bulgaria. Ferdinand I was born as the son of the Austrian General August von Sachsen-Coburg and Gotha. In 1887 he became ruler of Bulgaria after the abdication of Alexander I von Battenberg. In 1908 he made himself Tsar of Bulgaria. Because he joined the German and Austrian monarchy in WWI and lost the war, he had to abdicate on 3 October 1918 and to emigrate to Germany and Slovakia. In 1948 Ferdinand I of Bulgaria died in Coburg, Germany.

2107c2f5-2fd6-5b2a-8227-d2730838e6b4.name: École Polytechnique du Bardo
2107c2f5-2fd6-5b2a-8227-d2730838e6b4.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
2107c2f5-2fd6-5b2a-8227-d2730838e6b4.history: Founded in 1837 and opened on the 5 March 1840 by order of the bey, the École Polytechnique du Bardo was the first military academy in Ottoman Tunisia. Conscious of Christian Europe's military superiority and following the example of the Ottoman Tanzimat reforms, Ahmed Pacha Bey set out to "modernise" the state and the army. The school was directed by an Italian Orientalist, the Colonel Luigi Calligaris with the help of a Tunisian scholar, Sheikh Mahmoud Kabadu. The state was forced to shut down the school in 1868 due to lack of funds. It educated the first generation of Tunisian who weren't hostile to the West.
2107c2f5-2fd6-5b2a-8227-d2730838e6b4.description2: Located inside the Palais du Bardo, this school offered a six year course to any 15 to 20 year old student who could pass its rigorous selection process. The best students would then go on to complete their studies at the École Saint-Cyr in France. The English, French and Italian professors here taught sciences as well as literature and French and Italian. The top students had their first real test when they were called to fight in the Crimean war of October 1854, and later in the resistance to the French occupation in 1881. Today, the school is located opposite the Musée du Bardo, and has preserved is grandiose façade decorated with Italian marble and the beylical coat of arms.

22dc6a43-58e7-5410-b11f-2c3a946ecbb5.name: St. Cyprien. Post office. School.
22dc6a43-58e7-5410-b11f-2c3a946ecbb5.second_name: Société des Fermes Françaises de Tunisie
22dc6a43-58e7-5410-b11f-2c3a946ecbb5.description2: French agriculture in Tunisia began either through the establishment of large properties by private initiatives, or the introduction of settlers by the public authorities. This photograph shows us an example from the "first phase" - one of the "companies" (of "French farms") had purchased a large plot of land, and employed a number of (largely Arab and Italian) workers to cultivate the land.  Pictured is a school, whose director also worked as the post officer, a vital service for those who wished to communicate with their families back home.

22e62379-2fd3-551c-8a81-3883d3d21495.name: The biweekly paper *Spettatore Egiziano* was the first Italian-language newspaper to be published in Egypt
22e62379-2fd3-551c-8a81-3883d3d21495.author: Massimo Sanacore
22e62379-2fd3-551c-8a81-3883d3d21495.archival: ASLi, Governo civile e militare, b. 451
22e62379-2fd3-551c-8a81-3883d3d21495.third_name: *Spettatore egiziano. Giornale politico, scientifico, letterario e commerciale*
22e62379-2fd3-551c-8a81-3883d3d21495.description2:
The *Spettatore Egiziano* was founded in 1845 by Giacomo Castelnuovo, a Jewish medical doctor from Livorno (Tuscany, Italy) who had to flee his country in 1843 because of his affiliation to the Giovane Italia (the Italian patriotic and republican movement created by Giuseppe Mazzini). The *Spettatore Egiziano* was the first Italian-language newspaper to be published in Egypt. Castelnuovo also founded the *Il Progresso d’Egitto*, a bulletin that kept the Italian community in Egypt updated about the Italian political events like the 1848 revolutions.  
Castelnuovo later moved to Tunis where he became the Bey's physician.

2380f8f7-c82d-5b63-945d-edf979f223ee.name: Appraisal by the assessor of the Tribunal of Booty (Tribunale delle prede) of Palermo, of 25 'Turks of the Barbary Coast' captured by Italian corsairs from the Kingdom of Sicily and detained in Palermo
2380f8f7-c82d-5b63-945d-edf979f223ee.author: Renata De Simone
2380f8f7-c82d-5b63-945d-edf979f223ee.archival: ASPa, Consultore del Governo, Tribunale delle prede, vol. 268, carte senza numerazione
2380f8f7-c82d-5b63-945d-edf979f223ee.description2: In this document the assessor of the Booty Tribunal of Palermo explains that the magistrate has declared the booty captured by the captain corsair Domenico Pantò e Trifone Citarrella to be legitimate; they had plundered a Turkish boat and captured 25 Turks from the Barbary Coast. Upon request of the ship-owner, the assessor has been charged to appraise the value of the captives, so that they could be sold at auction. The captives included an entire family of “Barbary Turks”, composed of Salem, “husband” (60 years old, valued at 60 piastres), Cadduccia, “mother” (48 years old, 80 piastres), Agmet, “brother” (24 years old, 80 piastes), Lima, a 21 year old widow with her 2 year old son Ali, together valued at 100 piastres, and a 14 year old black servant called Fatuma, valued at only 20 piastres. Seven of the other captives were sailors, aged from 23 to 60 years old and valued a price ranging from 25 to 50 piastres, and two were passengers, whose commercial value was estimated at between 30 and 40 piastres.

24505a53-36c5-5b4a-9423-5215da35cb9b.name: *The Café des Platanes*
24505a53-36c5-5b4a-9423-5215da35cb9b.author: Dalila Orfali
24505a53-36c5-5b4a-9423-5215da35cb9b.keywords: Orientalism; traditional city; traditional urban space; colonial city
24505a53-36c5-5b4a-9423-5215da35cb9b.description2: This famous café is located by a fountain bearing the same name, built by the Dey Hassan. From 1832 it faced the Jardin d'Essai, giving it a view of this beautiful green space in the Hamma neighbourhood. This café and its fountain were immortalised by a number of painters. Various 17th century texts recall its peaceful atmosphere.

248b6ee3-8b98-5fe8-a126-461e9a621403.name: The Committee of Tunis for Milan Exhibition 1906
248b6ee3-8b98-5fe8-a126-461e9a621403.author: Giulia Barrera
248b6ee3-8b98-5fe8-a126-461e9a621403.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 5.
248b6ee3-8b98-5fe8-a126-461e9a621403.third_name: *Comitato di Tunisi per l'Esposizione di Milano 1906*
248b6ee3-8b98-5fe8-a126-461e9a621403.description2: The Italian community in Tunisia participated in the 1906 Milan international exhibition. The Committee in charge of organizing exhibition participation included Italian professionals and entrepreneurs who had migrated from Italy to Tunisia or who were children or grandchildren of immigrants, such as Alfredo Coen (owner of the furniture shop “Au Palais Arabe” and of a furniture factory), G. Di Vittorio and L. Rey (owners of constructions companies that built important public and private buildings, Di Vittorio, from Sicily, Rey, the child of an immigrant from Piedmont), Ugo Moreno (a trader, whose the family had migrated from Livorno in 1830) and Doctor Pietro Brignone (who ran a pharmacy in Tunis).

2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.name: The Great Mosque and University of Zaytuna
2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.history: Located in the heart of the Tunis medina, the great Zaytuna Mosque is the largest and most revered religious site in Tunis. City life revolved around this mosque, as it was not only an important place of worship, but also a great university, with a reputation matching that of the Qaraouyine University in Fez and the al-Azhar University in Cairo. Many theologians and scholars of literature, arts and sciences were trained here for generations. Although it was the subject of many reforms in the 19th century, the modern Zaytuna University still provides a religious education, and attracts many believers at prayer times.
2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.description2: An important place of worship, the Zaytuna mosque was subject to a great number of adjustments and expansions since its construction in the 7th century, most notably during the 17th and 18th centuries. The central courtyard is accessible through a suspended portico with horseshoe archways resting on beautiful columns topped with Hafsid capitals, through which the beautiful painted wooden ceilings can be seen. The paved courtyard is dominated by a square minaret, a beautiful sundial and a ribbed calotte which rests on an octagonal base above on a larger, square base. The décor is reminiscent of the Dome of the Rock in al-Quds (Jerusalem) in Palestine.

26fd8fdd-9bc0-5670-be93-f86c07c23383.name: Dresser
26fd8fdd-9bc0-5670-be93-f86c07c23383.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
26fd8fdd-9bc0-5670-be93-f86c07c23383.description2: This wooden dresser contains four large drawers and one thin upper drawer. It is topped with a marble slab and rectangular mirror in a wooden frame, decorated with a wooden crest and carved with floral patterns. The wood is covered in a mosaic of bone or ceramic pieces, organised in a floral design. Each drawer has a keyhole and is opened by two individually painted knobs.

2739eecb-f1a1-5544-8ead-dcf31ff17148.name: An elderly Paul Draneht (1815–94) with his daughter Despina
2739eecb-f1a1-5544-8ead-dcf31ff17148.author: Massimiliano Cremona, Ignazio Galella
2739eecb-f1a1-5544-8ead-dcf31ff17148.description2: In 1894, Paul Draneht, who had been awarded the title of Pasha, died in Alexandria. His daughter Despina married a Greek businessman, Emmanuel Zervudachi, and the family continued to be part of a Mediterranean cosmopolitan elite.

27da4fd7-996d-5066-b357-ffc4082c83ad.name: Dr Charles Nicolle
27da4fd7-996d-5066-b357-ffc4082c83ad.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
27da4fd7-996d-5066-b357-ffc4082c83ad.description2: This is a photograph of the Nobel Prize for Medicine won by Dr Charles Nicolle for his work on infectious illnesses during his time at l'Institut Pasteur from 1903 to 1936.

28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.name: Grand Bazar Arabe. A late-19th-century bazaar built in Tunis by the construction company of G. Di Vittorio, an Italian immigrant in Tunisia
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.dates: Photograph: first years of the 20th century; building: late 19th century
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.author: Giulia Barrera
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 189
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.third_name: *Grand Bazar Arabe. G. Di Vittorio imprenditore. Tunisi*
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.description2:
On the main entrance one can read the shop sign “Grand Bazar Kassar Said”; on the left “Grand Bazar Arab” and on the right, one can read the shop sign “I. Piperno”: Piperno is an unmistakably Italian Jewish name.  
Giuseppe Di Vittorio, who ran the construction company that built this building, migrated from Termini Imerese (a small town near Palermo, Sicily, Italy) in 1882.

28712296-3b43-5ca3-b4e9-c6cec4c1ce1a.name: Revolver
28712296-3b43-5ca3-b4e9-c6cec4c1ce1a.type: Military object; metalwork; firearms; arms and armour
28712296-3b43-5ca3-b4e9-c6cec4c1ce1a.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
28712296-3b43-5ca3-b4e9-c6cec4c1ce1a.keywords: Military object; Metalwork; Cast steel; Arms and armour; Wooden grip plates
28712296-3b43-5ca3-b4e9-c6cec4c1ce1a.description2: Yusuf Bey Karam's revolver, which he used in the resistance against the Ottomans. It is made of cast steel and fitted with a wooden grip.

28f6f7de-3daa-59e6-960d-f0cac66b210d.name: North African caravan, in the west of the Sahara
28f6f7de-3daa-59e6-960d-f0cac66b210d.third_name: A Travers le Monde, Paris: Hachette, 1895–1914
28f6f7de-3daa-59e6-960d-f0cac66b210d.description2: Camille Douls (1864–1889), who was passionate  about Africa, decided in the late 19th century to enter indigenous North African territory, despite it being forbidden for foreigners at the time. He began to learn Arabic and study the Quran for this purpose, and was able to live among the Oulad Delim tribe for five months, although not without risk to his personal safety. He published his observations on his return (1888), which attracted much attention, as no European had lived among these people to date. He was assassinated the following year during a trip to Algeria. The tale of his time in the desert was illustrated by Jules Girardet, an artist specialising in historical scenes who had never seen the subjects of his drawings. This image is therefore interesting, as it sheds light on the nature of the stereotypical Western gaze on nomadic lifestyles.

29092d3e-f7b7-5e75-a750-72b4e7e7bbd1.name: *Fugitives Of Herzegovina*
29092d3e-f7b7-5e75-a750-72b4e7e7bbd1.author: Petar Petrovic
29092d3e-f7b7-5e75-a750-72b4e7e7bbd1.description2: In response to events in the Serbo-Turkish war of 1875-78, Uroš Predić presents his extremely realistic treatment of a subject glorifying not the heroic struggle for liberation, but the hardships of innocent people forced to go into hiding. The artist was inspired by similar works with historical subjects, like those painted by Jaroslav Čermak (1831-1878), but painted his figures from live models, mostly close relatives who posed for him in a Belgrade studio. Thanks to the world-renowned scientist and benefactor Mihailo Pupin (1854-1935), *Fugitives of Herzegovina* became a part of the collection of the National Museum in Belgrade in 1923.

2a4f3434-97f1-53a2-837d-e4407a1a20de.name: Dagger
2a4f3434-97f1-53a2-837d-e4407a1a20de.type: Military object; metalwork; arms and armour
2a4f3434-97f1-53a2-837d-e4407a1a20de.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
2a4f3434-97f1-53a2-837d-e4407a1a20de.keywords: Military object; Metalwork; Arms; armour; Steel
2a4f3434-97f1-53a2-837d-e4407a1a20de.description2: These small daggers were used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. This dagger is an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. The blade is made of steel and has a curved double-edge. The handle is made of wood and painted black, with decorative drawings in gold paint.

2b174c47-ca5a-5be5-853f-ba97cf7eac1e.name: Carthage Cathedral
2b174c47-ca5a-5be5-853f-ba97cf7eac1e.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
2b174c47-ca5a-5be5-853f-ba97cf7eac1e.history: This old Catholic cathedral is located on the Byrsa Hill, near the Carthage archaeological site. It was built by the King of France in honour of his grandfather, King Louis IX, in the very place he had died of the plague. The cathedral is also evidence of the Tunisian beys' tolerance and their help in protecting the Christian religion in the Regency of Tunis in the 19th century. Building works began in 1884, and it was consecrated by the French Protectorate on 15 May 1890. It became the primatial cathedral of Africa once the title of The Primate of Africa was returned to the Cardinal Lavigerie, who was also the Archidiocese of Algiers and Carthage. It was no longer used as a place of worship after Tunisian independence, and has become an important landmark for tourism and culture, having been renamed the Acropolium de Carthage in 1993.
2b174c47-ca5a-5be5-853f-ba97cf7eac1e.keywords: Architecture; Romano-Byzanine style; vaults; stained-glass windows; tapestry; marble
2b174c47-ca5a-5be5-853f-ba97cf7eac1e.description2: The Saint-Louis de Carthage Cathedral was built on the top the Byrsa Hill, the highest point in Punic Carthage, on the site of the Roman Capitol over an area of 1,800 m2. It is built in a North African Byzantine style, supported by 174 marble columns with golden capitals and wooden painted ceilings imported from Europe and carved with arabesques. Inside the cathedral, the choir rises in the shape of two semi-circular arches, covered by a sky-blue dome. It is built with three naves and has an ambulatory on the first floor. Light shines through 284 stained-glass windows decorated with arabesques, with those on the central nave depicting Saint Louis and Saint Augustine, the cathedral's two patron saints.

2b9bd4b7-9bf4-5be0-b693-18e62b5dc6f7.name: Drinking cup
2b9bd4b7-9bf4-5be0-b693-18e62b5dc6f7.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities
2b9bd4b7-9bf4-5be0-b693-18e62b5dc6f7.author: Huda Kilani
2b9bd4b7-9bf4-5be0-b693-18e62b5dc6f7.keywords: Stepped pedestal; silver; geometric decoration; Caucasian immigrants; domestic vessels
2b9bd4b7-9bf4-5be0-b693-18e62b5dc6f7.description2: Small silver cup with a stepped pedestal for drinking hard liquors. The surface is decorated with geometric designs, including dots, lines and triangles. On the upper part of the cup, an engraved inscription in Russian ("your health") runs along the external surface. The year of manufacture (1896) is stamped. Items like this were brought to Jordan in the last quarter of the 19th century by Caucasian immigrants, the Circassians. The immigration of the Circassians started in the middle of nineteenth century and continued until 1900. They migrated to the eastern Arab countries with which they have spiritual and religious links. This object illustrates the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and the various local costumes, crafts and rites.

2efb58fe-14fe-59df-ad70-18b84374d4f5.name: Edmund Count Szechenyi (1839–1922)
2efb58fe-14fe-59df-ad70-18b84374d4f5.description2: Portrait of Count Edmund Szechenyi. He was born in 1839 in Bratislava and studied the work of fire brigades in London. In 1869 he founded in Budapest the first volunteer fire brigade, which was transformed into a professional fire brigade in 1870. From 1871–1874 he commanded the umbrella organisation of all fire brigades in Hungary. In 1875 he was sent by Emperor Franz Joseph to Istanbul to build up a fire brigade in the Ottoman capital. As head of the fire brigade he became the first Christian Pasha in the Ottoman Army and stayed in Istanbul until his death in 1922.

2fa02ca6-7ad8-55e1-8e26-60c11f068f26.name: Letter from the Dey of Algiers, Muhammad Pasha, to Ferdinando IV of Bourbon, King of Naples, granting a two-month truce from corsairs’ attacks (in Arabic with Italian translation)
2fa02ca6-7ad8-55e1-8e26-60c11f068f26.author: Rossana Spadaccini
2fa02ca6-7ad8-55e1-8e26-60c11f068f26.archival: AS NA, Ministero degli affari esteri, 4212
2fa02ca6-7ad8-55e1-8e26-60c11f068f26.description2: The Dey of Algiers wrote that he graciously granted to the King of Naples a two-month truce (for April and May of 1787). If his corsairs met ships belonging to the Kingdom of Naples, they would not attack them. The two nations would treat each other “with mutual friendship”.

30cc5fa9-8b03-5f71-9493-92a9a15324e0.name: Migration preparations from Lemnos island to Turkey
30cc5fa9-8b03-5f71-9493-92a9a15324e0.holder: Population Exchange Museum (The Foundation of Lausanne Treaty Emigrants)
30cc5fa9-8b03-5f71-9493-92a9a15324e0.description2: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. During the migration waves during the 1896-97 riots in Crete, 40,000 Cretan Muslims had to migrate to territories under Ottoman rule: Lebanon, Syria and Anatolia. This photograph pertains to migration preparations from Lemnos to Turkey in 1924.

3145dc39-d491-535e-aaa2-6545cc31f4e7.name: Chair of Krste Petkov Misirkov
3145dc39-d491-535e-aaa2-6545cc31f4e7.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
3145dc39-d491-535e-aaa2-6545cc31f4e7.description2: Misirkov’s book “On Macedonian Matters” lays the foundations of the modern Macedonian language and grammar. Being one of the central figures of the “Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society" in St. Petersburg, he largely contributed to issuing the periodical Macedonian and Russian-language publication, “Makedonski Golos” (“Macedonian Voice").

31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.name: Statue of Cardinal Lavigerie
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.author: Bechir Yazidi
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.keywords: French protectorate of Tunisia; missionaries in Tunisia
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.description2: On the 23 November 1925, the French resident-general in Tunisia, Lucien Saint, organised a solemn gathering to commemorate 100 years since Cardinal Lavigerie's birth. The municipality of Tunis also received a statue of him brandishing a cross by the sculptor Élie-Jean Vézien, which they chose to put in Place Bab el-Bhar (at the entrance to the medina), a place of great importance to Tunisians. This choice of location angered the Tunisian population and triggered a protest from the students of the Zaytuna University, who considered this act an attack on their religious beliefs (it was placed close to the Zaytuna Mosque) and their traditions. The statue stayed there until Tunisian independence, when it was removed by the Mayor of Tunis.  Lavigerie was the Archbishop of Algiers and Carthage, and the founder of the Pères Blancs in 1868.

33430dbe-c0fc-5bb4-9845-6bce853a6ea6.name: General Hullin's audience, provided by the Dey of Algeria
33430dbe-c0fc-5bb4-9845-6bce853a6ea6.description2: In August 1802, irritated by the repeated pillaging of his ships by Algerian pirates, Napoléon I sent General Hullin and Consul Dubois-Thainville to the then Dey of Algeria, Mustafa Pasha, with a threatening message. This print is an example of Napoleonic propaganda, as it attempts to highlight the "insolence" of the bey, who stays seated on the sofa, and the "bravery" of the general who, with a sword on his side, makes his speech.

3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.name: The female surgery division of the Italian hospital in Tunis
3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.author: Giulia Barrera
3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906. p. 84
3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.description2:
Prior to the establishment of the French protectorate on Tunisia in 1881, Italian doctors operated in Tunisia. The Bey had frequently employed Italian physicians. Some were born in Tunisia, of Jewish families from Livorno, others had arrived in Tunisia as political exiles in the first half of the 19th century. The largest contingent of Italian doctors, however, migrated to Tunisia after 1881.  
In 1890, the Italian community opened a hospital with about 100 beds. Italian physicians worked in the hospital as volunteers and indigent patients were treated for free. The initial funding for creating and running the hospital came from the Italian community; the Italian state contributed to pay the expenses for the construction of a new facility in 1900 and partly subsidized the hospital activities.

en: Pendola, M., *Gli italiani di Tunisia: storia di una comunità (XIX-XX secolo)*, Foligno: Editoriale Umbra, 2007.

351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.name: Au Palais Arabe. A furniture shop of the Italians Eugenio and Alfredo Coen in Tunis
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.dates: Photograph: first years of the 20th century; building: late 19th–early 20th century
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.author: Giulia Barrera
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 164
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.description2: “Au Palais Arabe”, Rue de Rome, 3, Tunis, was once the most important shop in town for furniture and other household items. Eugenio Coen (born in Livorno in 1855, migrated to Tunis in 1885) and his brother Alfredo (born in Livorno in 1868 and migrated to Tunis in 1887) also ran a furniture factory that, in 1906, employed about 100 carpenters, cabinet makers and other workers, 80 per cent of whom were Italian.

35b961a6-875c-5ccf-a80f-d6f917ccd48e.name: Jozef Zachariasz Bem (1795–1850)
35b961a6-875c-5ccf-a80f-d6f917ccd48e.keywords: Jozef Zachariasz Bem; Aleppo; Syria; Hungary
35b961a6-875c-5ccf-a80f-d6f917ccd48e.description2: Portrait of Jozef Zachariasz Bem as Turkish Pasha. Jozef Bem was born in the Austrian part of Poland. He fought as a Napoleonic officer against the Russians. In 1830 he participated in the Polish uprising against the Russians in Warsaw. In 1848 he was one of the leading Generals fighting with the Hungarian army against the Habsburg troops. After several defeats in 1849, he fled with 6,000 Hungarian-Polish soldiers to the Ottoman Empire. After converting to Islam, he became a Turkish General. In 1850 he suppressed an Arabic pogrom against the Christian population of Aleppo.

3684ea69-4081-5b3d-99c4-ac49b735a423.name: *L’escalier des lions* (painting)
3684ea69-4081-5b3d-99c4-ac49b735a423.holder: Palais de la Rose – Musée de l’Armée
3684ea69-4081-5b3d-99c4-ac49b735a423.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
3684ea69-4081-5b3d-99c4-ac49b735a423.keywords: Palais du Bardo; capitals; ceramic panels; Andalusian style
3684ea69-4081-5b3d-99c4-ac49b735a423.materials: Canvas, wood, coloured pigments, gold leaf
3684ea69-4081-5b3d-99c4-ac49b735a423.description2: This important painting depicts the official entrance of the Palais du Bardo as it was originally, with the *escalier des lions* and Mohamed Sadok Bey exiting the palace in official uniform, accompanied by Tunisian dignitaries, preceded by protocol officers and surrounded by the beylical guard. It shows the monumental *escalier des lions* with its archways and columns on the façade. We can also see its glorious white marble columns, capitals and ceramic panels decorating the walls and mounted on plaster and stucco (*naqsh hadida*). Through the entrance doors the black and white archways in an Andalusian style can be seen on the first floor.

37704ccd-a34d-52a2-84f8-9695829027c7.name: Jewellery for horses – Type 1
37704ccd-a34d-52a2-84f8-9695829027c7.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
37704ccd-a34d-52a2-84f8-9695829027c7.keywords: Decoration; Silver; Silver chains; Jewels; Precious stones
37704ccd-a34d-52a2-84f8-9695829027c7.description2: These strings of jewels were used on the horses of Ottoman officials and indicated their high status and wealth. The chain consists of a small, red coral, semi-precious gemstones and silver pendants which would bounce against each other to create a tinkling noise and announce the arrival of the rider.

3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.name: Egyptian Furniture of the Italian Giuseppe Parvis Living in Cairo [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.author: Marina Minozzi
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.archival: *L'Esposizione di Parigi del 1878 illustrata*, Sonzogno Editore, 1878, p. 632.
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.keywords: International exhibition; universal exposition; Exposition universelle de Paris; pavillion; social change; applied arts; model; Moorish style; house; middle class; market; trade; Italian craftsmanship; Italians in Egypt; artistic exchange
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.copyright: Copyright image: Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Roma.
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.third_name: *Mobili egiziani del'italiano Giuseppe Parvis dimorante al Cairo*
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.description2: Giuseppe Parvis, who emigrated from Italy to Egypt, began extensive production of elegant furniture adapted to Arabian taste and decorated with mother-of-pearl and metal inserts. He won awards for his work at the Universal Exhibitions of Paris in 1867, Vienna and Philadelphia. Giuseppe Parvis is an example of successful businessman who successfully adapted to the Egyptian market. He was able to run laboratories with 50 workers and trained a large number of students in ebony furniture making. Over the span of 20 years he introduced and sold furniture to Arabian people who traditionally did not possess such furniture, using an Arabic style and taste and by using woods found in the East, Egypt and China.

390fed84-29b4-5b5f-8552-8a2d440391d6.name: *Colonial Education*
390fed84-29b4-5b5f-8552-8a2d440391d6.description2: This article on the "colonial education" the youth received in France, published in a newspaper for the French community in Tunisia, has a didactic objective, encouraging and legitimising French economic colonialism in Tunisia, and thus also the migration of French youth to Tunisia.

3948e69b-7a69-50c3-8b58-824c4c6e5d46.name: Moods: Those Who Go
3948e69b-7a69-50c3-8b58-824c4c6e5d46.author: Marina Minozzi
3948e69b-7a69-50c3-8b58-824c4c6e5d46.keywords: Migration; Italian migration; Italian painters; painting; sculpture; realism; artistic exchanges; Filippo Tommaso Marinetti; Futurismo; Futurism; unification of Italy; social history; social topics; Italian society; post-unitarian Italian society
3948e69b-7a69-50c3-8b58-824c4c6e5d46.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
3948e69b-7a69-50c3-8b58-824c4c6e5d46.description2: Umberto Bocccioni moved to Rome in 1901 where he was interested in painting, journalism and literature. Through his friendship with Severini, Boccioni attended Balla’s atelier and, at the same time, the school of nude of the Academy of Fine Arts in Rome. In 1907 he moved to Milan and met Previati and Marinetti, who wrote the Manifest of Futurism. In 1910 he signed the Manifest of Futurist Painters, in 1912 he signed the Manifest of Futurist Sculpture. His studies of Munch and Previati influenced the cycle called Moods. He starts doing numerous preparatory studies for the triptych: *Farewell, Those Who Go, Those Who Stay*; in which he set a correspondence between, colours, lines and feelings, moods. The painting is one of the studies for the series *Those Who Go* that belong to the first of two trilogies about Moods created in 1911, before the artist moved to Paris.

3a479e74-ad19-5334-a508-9d331c6ee9bd.name: 'Air force'
3a479e74-ad19-5334-a508-9d331c6ee9bd.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History

3a479e74-ad19-5334-a508-9d331c6ee9bd.description2: In 1911, in Libya, the newly founded Italian Air Force carried out the very first aerial bombing of civilian targets in world history. Italian anti-colonialists vocally protested such practice, as Scalarini’s cartoon shows.

3b50b4cf-8492-533e-8f06-4e7806420158.name: Tsar Nikolai and his family visit Queen Victoria
3b50b4cf-8492-533e-8f06-4e7806420158.keywords: Diplomacy; Russia; England; Nicholas II; Victoria
3b50b4cf-8492-533e-8f06-4e7806420158.description2: Alix de Hesse-Darmstadt, who became the last Empress of Russia under the name Alexandra Romanova, was the granddaughter of none other than Queen Victoria of England. Nikolai II and his wife Alexandra stopped off in England on the way to Paris for their official trip in 1896, to introduce their first child (Olga) to her great-grandmother, Queen Victoria.  This photo is more of a family portrait than an official image.

3d30eac6-fec9-5efa-aa61-82d8011a50af.name: Italian Workers Friendly Society (Tunis)
3d30eac6-fec9-5efa-aa61-82d8011a50af.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 41
3d30eac6-fec9-5efa-aa61-82d8011a50af.third_name: *Società operaia italiana di mutuo soccorso. Tunisi*
3d30eac6-fec9-5efa-aa61-82d8011a50af.description2: The Italian Workers Friendly Society was only one of the many organizations that the Italian migrants set up in Tunisia, ranging from the Chamber of Commerce, to Masonic Lodges, to religious organisations, to cultural associations and political groups.

3f284929-6dd8-5a5b-9540-23005e47ac6c.name: Colonial school in Paris, project of M. Maurice Yvon
3f284929-6dd8-5a5b-9540-23005e47ac6c.second_name: *Longitudinal view; Plan of the first floor*
3f284929-6dd8-5a5b-9540-23005e47ac6c.description2: In 1885, the French diplomat Auguste Pavie brought thirteen young Khmers to Paris so that they could see France. This "Cambodian mission" was soon transformed into a colonial school which accepted young students of French, Cambodian or African origins in order to train the future civil servants of the colonies. Over first two, then three, years the students studied a variety of languages, French law, and ethnology. in 1895 the architect Maurice Yvon, son of an Orientalist painter, was appointed as the architect for a specialist school on 2 Rue de l'Observatoire. Insipired by "neo-Moorish" architecture, the resulting structure became a key example of "colonial art".

4015cd67-07da-50de-ad09-a73de96638ef.name: Abdul Baha Abbas (1844–1921)
4015cd67-07da-50de-ad09-a73de96638ef.description2: Born in Tehran, Abbas left Iran because of religious persecution. He travelled widely in Egypt, Europe and the United States. In 1913 he settled in Haifa where he founded the religious sect of Baha'i.

40ef2328-28fd-59f1-96b3-b75abf4e6c58.name: *Bedouin of the Houran*
40ef2328-28fd-59f1-96b3-b75abf4e6c58.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
40ef2328-28fd-59f1-96b3-b75abf4e6c58.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
40ef2328-28fd-59f1-96b3-b75abf4e6c58.description2: The constant movement of large Bedouin confederations regularly impacted on the history of the Middle East, in particular when it intersected with settled societies and cities. The bedouins of Hauran lived in the Hauran plain in what is now SW Syria/ NW Jordan at the time. The Sheikh of the Hauran bedouins was employed by the Ottoman pasha of Damascus to collect tribute from all tribes in the area and help in its defence. Philip Meeder was a British wood engraver, who died in 1913. The image is taken from ’Picturesque Palestine, Sinai and Egypt’, Charles William Wilson ed., 1881. The accompanying text in the book reads: 'A bedouin of the Haurân. Bedouins occupy the north-west district of the Haurân; the plain is inhabited by peasants, and the Druses for many centuries have colonised the mountain range.

41adce0c-3867-5629-8e66-064e9b952e0c.name: Refugees' documents for refuge house after the population exchange
41adce0c-3867-5629-8e66-064e9b952e0c.holder: Population Exchange Museum (The Foundation of Lausanne Treaty Emigrants)
41adce0c-3867-5629-8e66-064e9b952e0c.description2: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. These are refugees' documents for the Papoukidis family's stay at a refuge house.

43b2594e-92cf-584f-b624-afc4b94a968d.name: Giovanni Miani (1810–1872)
43b2594e-92cf-584f-b624-afc4b94a968d.description2: Portrait of Giovanni Miani (1810–1872). Born in Northern Italy, he was an intellectual who was forced by Austrian authorities to seek exile in the Ottoman Empire. He lived in Athens, Smyrna and Egypt and was one of the European explorers who tried to find the sources of the Nile.

453156d3-f141-581a-96a5-4ef8c83cbae1.name: Dr Charles Nicolle
453156d3-f141-581a-96a5-4ef8c83cbae1.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
453156d3-f141-581a-96a5-4ef8c83cbae1.description2: Pictured here is Dr. Charles Nicolle, a French microbiology doctor born in Rouen on 21 September 1966, in his research laboratory. His name is strongly linked to l'Institut Pasteur, which he directed from 1903–1936, playing the role of administrator, researcher, school headmaster, and advocate for the teaching of hygiene and illness prevention. In 1928 he received the Nobel Prize for Physiology. He died in 1936 and is buried at the Institut Pasteur, where his tombstone is engraved with olive and apple tree branches crossed over, the symbols of Tunisia and Normandy.

4590fdc2-d3b9-5462-8feb-df1ae40b4e9e.name: *Lesson at the Benaki Orphanage in Alexandria Egypt*
4590fdc2-d3b9-5462-8feb-df1ae40b4e9e.author: Maria Dimitriadou
4590fdc2-d3b9-5462-8feb-df1ae40b4e9e.description2: Geometry lesson in Benakio Orphanage in Alexandria. Photographer Asiz e Dores.

460ecb9a-1f86-59fa-b384-df26f5b5b4fa.name: The Chinese quarter at Cormeilles-en-Parisis
460ecb9a-1f86-59fa-b384-df26f5b5b4fa.description2: The first wave of Chinese immigration to France was in 1916, when the Chinese government signed a treaty to send 35,000 Chinese citizens to work in France. This first small group, who had settled mainly in the regions around Paris, was followed by a second wave in the 1930s. Badly paid, and living in makeshift accommodation, these Chinese immigrants were mostly given heavy manual work.

46d97a8f-bb71-5869-a2ce-ba8b09411232.name: Bond of 100 francs issued by the Caisse Générale de Secours et de Bienfaisance Israélite de Tunis, in order to raise funds for the construction of a new synagogue in Tunis, and bought by Leone Moreno
46d97a8f-bb71-5869-a2ce-ba8b09411232.author: Massimo Sanacore
46d97a8f-bb71-5869-a2ce-ba8b09411232.archival: ASLi, Archivio Moreno di Tunisi, b. 12
46d97a8f-bb71-5869-a2ce-ba8b09411232.description2:
The construction of the Great Synagogue in Tunis had a long and complicated history. In 1883, the Bey granted a plot of land on which to build the temple to the Italian Jewish physician and president of the Alliance Israélite Universelle of Tunis, Giacomo Castelnuovo. However, the synagogue was ultimately built on a different lot, acquired thanks to a private donation. In the first years of the 20th century, different projects were discussed. The synagogue was finally built in the 1930s.  
  
Leone Moreno (Tunis 1852 – Tunis 1950) was a successful Italian entrepreneur. He belonged to a Jewish family that had migrated from Livorno (Tuscany) to Tunis around 1830. He was awarded honours both by the Italian King (Cavaliere dell’Ordine della Corona d’Italia) and by the Bey of Tunis (Nichan Iftikhar).

477c2b68-4a2a-5890-9452-4710f4eee340.name: Jewellery for horses – Type 2
477c2b68-4a2a-5890-9452-4710f4eee340.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
477c2b68-4a2a-5890-9452-4710f4eee340.description2: These strings of jewels were used on the horses of Ottoman officials and indicated their high status and wealth. The chain consists of a variety of differently shaped beads which would bounce against each other to create a tinkling noise and announce the arrival of the rider.

47bb854c-9eb2-5d07-b0f1-7d41e63b0500.name: *The Qadous path*
47bb854c-9eb2-5d07-b0f1-7d41e63b0500.author: Dalila Orfali
47bb854c-9eb2-5d07-b0f1-7d41e63b0500.description2: The clever use of light in this painting helps illustrate the beauty of the countryside around Algiers in the 19th century. It highlights the richness of the vegetation in the area surrounding the Algerian notability's country homes.

47de166a-64f2-5809-807d-457eb735b800.name: Stefan Petrovic Knicanin (1809–1855)
47de166a-64f2-5809-807d-457eb735b800.description2: Portrait of Stefan Petrovic Knicanin. The Serbian officer Stefan Petrovic Knicanin supported the Austrian Emperor during the 1848 revolution. In 1849 he returned to Serbia and fostered good relations between Serbia and Austria. He died in 1855 in Belgrade.

47e09866-3a31-5ee5-a109-a01ff8ff7576.name: *Treaty of Peace and Trade between France and the Tunisian Regency*
47e09866-3a31-5ee5-a109-a01ff8ff7576.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
47e09866-3a31-5ee5-a109-a01ff8ff7576.description2: The Treaty of Peace and Trade, signed between France and the Tunisian Regency, was written in both French and Arabic. It protected all French ships from attacks from Tunisian privateers, gave them access to every port in the country, and guaranteed all French nationals full security.

47f1e835-2989-56cc-b52c-52619991c2a5.name: Italian military conscription office in Tunis
47f1e835-2989-56cc-b52c-52619991c2a5.author: Massimo Sanacore
47f1e835-2989-56cc-b52c-52619991c2a5.archival: ASLi, Famiglia Moreno di Tunisi, b. 15
47f1e835-2989-56cc-b52c-52619991c2a5.description2: Under terms of an 1896 agreement with France, Italy ran a military conscription office in Tunis. It was through this office that Italy drafted its migrants in Tunisia for the war on Turkey in 1911-12 and for the First World War. During WWI, many Italians living in Tunisia, because of their knowledge of the French language.  were assigned to the military units posted in France. Many of them died or were crippled for life. After the war, the Italian government opened a War Pensions Bureau in Tunis.

49a80737-c924-5479-8273-7392e3cd1db8.name: Gjorgij Pulevski
49a80737-c924-5479-8273-7392e3cd1db8.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
49a80737-c924-5479-8273-7392e3cd1db8.description2: Gjorgji Pulevski was a prominent figure of the Macedonian Enlightenment. He was born in Galichnik in 1822 and died in Sofia in 1893. In 1873, during his stay in Belgrade, he published the ”Dictionary of Four Languages,” which included Macedonian, Albanian, Greek and Turkish words. His “Dictionary of Three Languages” was issued in 1875. Gjorgji Pulevski was the founder of the Macedonian Literary Society, established in Sofia in 1888. It was one of the independent associations of Macedonian emigrants that made contributions to the awakening of the Macedonian national spirit.

4a2a96ac-fddb-5683-9208-73c5deb06b72.name: The Italian-language newspaper *L’Unione* (1886–1943), printed in Tunis
4a2a96ac-fddb-5683-9208-73c5deb06b72.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
4a2a96ac-fddb-5683-9208-73c5deb06b72.author: Giulia Barrera

4a2a96ac-fddb-5683-9208-73c5deb06b72.description2: Italian immigrants in Tunisia gave life to a vibrant press. Between 1838 and 1956, 123 Italian periodicals of different type were published in the country. *L’Unione* was the most successful and politically influential among them.

4a617bed-3c19-5563-b98a-4cd98cda144d.description: This painting was made around 1863 when the author travelled to Morocco with Mariano Fortuny. The reason of his travel was to paint the characters and “picturesque” garments as the way of life of the people from Morocco. His experiences can be seen in his paintings and drawings. During his travels he brought exotic artworks as Egyptian sarcophagi.
4a617bed-3c19-5563-b98a-4cd98cda144d.author: Carolina Miguel Arroyo

4ac252d2-71d1-5064-9680-d48fa70fd153.name: Colonial style building
4ac252d2-71d1-5064-9680-d48fa70fd153.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
4ac252d2-71d1-5064-9680-d48fa70fd153.history: In Tunis, the capital of the Protectorate imposed by France on Tunisia in 1881, the European quarter built itself right next to the old Arab medina. A new kind of home - the investment property - soon appeared, and the term balas (from the Italian palazzo) became widespread. These two or three-storey housing blocks greatly affected the city's urban landscape by introducing many different architectural styles as well as new architects, designers and builders with from different backgrounds. The 19th century was the century of eclecticism in Tunisia (both neo-classical and neo-baroque), whereas the 20th century was most marked by the influence of Art Nouveau.
4ac252d2-71d1-5064-9680-d48fa70fd153.description2:
As the name suggests, Palazzo de Guidi at 9 Rue d'Italie (now Rue Charles-de-Gaulle), was built in 1903–1906 by an Italian architect. The building has traces of different styles and influences (North African, Byzantine), and uses a variety of materials, such as stucco, mosaics, marquetery and ironwork, but as a whole it should be seen as a product of the Art Nouveau movement.  
  
The same trend of using byzantine and "oriental" motifs, but organised in a different way, is clear in the buildings at 18 and 20 Rue des Salines. Built in 1909–1910, these three-storey buildings reflect an attempt to bring together the styles of Neo-Classicism, Art Nouveau and "Arabisance", and the beautiful mosaics on the top floor with golden backgrounds are a perfect example of this.

4bccb3e9-a964-52ef-937f-7a6d6e11e5cf.name: *Interior of a house in Boussaada*
4bccb3e9-a964-52ef-937f-7a6d6e11e5cf.author: Dalila Orfali
4bccb3e9-a964-52ef-937f-7a6d6e11e5cf.description2: This painting, showing the interior of a traditional house in the Boussaada region, elicits a certain intimacy, recalling the muted atmosphere also evoked by Guillaumet's *Fileuse*. The nervous, moving brushstrokes and his use of melted or soldered lead are clear references to the style of the Dutch masters.

4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.name: The Italian woman poet and peace activist of Armenian descent Vittoria Aganoor Pompilj (1855–1910), and a signed copy of her poem 'Peace'
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.type: Photograph and autograph collected in a register
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.author: Maria Grazia Bistoni, Costanza Maria Del Giudice
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.archival: AS PG, Società per la pace e l'arbitrato internazionale di Perugia, 10
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.description2: The descendant of an Armenian family that migrated to Venice at the beginning of the 19th century, Vittoria Aganoor Pompilj authored poems that were translated during her life into English, French and Spanish. She corresponded with many international literary figures and was a member of the International Arbitration and Peace League of Perugia (*Società per la pace e l'arbitrato internazionale di Perugia*), founded in 1892. In 1870, the British trade unionist Randal Cremer (Nobel peace laureate in 1907) founded the International Arbitration League, which –among other things – protested British intervention in Egypt and imperialism.

4c84389a-5e72-52a7-92f3-aa8604a09e9c.name: Declaration by the Bey of Tunis assuring that in future wars with any European power prisoners will not be enslaved
4c84389a-5e72-52a7-92f3-aa8604a09e9c.author: Edoardo Garis, Giulia Barrera
4c84389a-5e72-52a7-92f3-aa8604a09e9c.archival: ASTo,Materie politiche per rapporto all'estero, Trattati diversi, mazzo 4 seconda addizione, fasc. 7
4c84389a-5e72-52a7-92f3-aa8604a09e9c.description2:
This declaration was an annex to a treaty between the King of Sardinia (who ruled over Piedmont, Genoa and Sardinia) and the Bey (who ruled Tunis), concluded by British Admiral Baron Exmouth, who lead a military expedition against the Berber states in 1816. The Bey declared that in case of future wars with any European power, “none of the prisoners made on either side shall be consigned to slavery, but treated with all humanity as prisoners of war, until regularly exchanged according to European practice”.  
The Exmouth expedition was aimed at stopping Barbary corsairs from raiding European shipping in the Mediterranean. At the time, privateering was considered a legitimate form of warfare by European and North African countries alike. Only in 1856 did France, the United Kingdom and other European powers (except from Spain) declare privateering illegal.

4fe44b43-1a7d-5881-a567-e328acd991f0.name: Tunis Cathedral
4fe44b43-1a7d-5881-a567-e328acd991f0.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
4fe44b43-1a7d-5881-a567-e328acd991f0.history: The Cathédrale Saint-Vincent-de-Paul is the active Catholic cathedral of Tunis. It is located on Place de l'Indépendance at the crossroads between the Avenue Habib-Bourguiba (previously Jules-Ferry) and the Avenue de France (previously the French general residence). Built between 1893 and 1897, it is named after the Saint Vincent de Paul, the founder of the Lazaristes and the Filles de la Charité, who was kidnapped as a young priest and sold as a slave in Tunisia in the early 7th century. The Modus Vivendi, signed in 1964 between independent Tunisia and the Vatican, ensured the cathedral became the property of the Roman Catholic Church. Today, the cathedral receives a great number of visitors and tourists, as well as important religious figures such as the Pope John Paul II in 1998.
4fe44b43-1a7d-5881-a567-e328acd991f0.keywords: Architecture; Romano-Byzantine style; vaults; stained-glass windows; tapestry; marble
4fe44b43-1a7d-5881-a567-e328acd991f0.description2: This cathedral was built on land given to the Christian community by the Bey of Tunis, and replaced the Église Sainte-Croix. The first stone was laid by Cardinal Lavigerie on the 7 November 1881, just after the establishment of French Protectorate. It was built in an austere Romano-Byzantine style with neo-classical influences, reflecting the monumental and majestic image of itself France presented to both its protégés and its rival powers. It contains huge statues of Christ, monumental vaults, stained-glass windows, tapestry, and marble columns. The organ inside the cathedral, built in 1921 by an expert from Paris and inaugurated on 28 October 1923, is considered to be the most beautiful organ in the African continent.

503f7b59-beb0-5c06-8952-0baa809cc018.name: *The arrival of the refugees*
503f7b59-beb0-5c06-8952-0baa809cc018.author: Maria Dimitriadou
503f7b59-beb0-5c06-8952-0baa809cc018.description2:
A black and white photo from an album depicting the arrival of Greek refugees after the Asia Minor catastrophe. Photographer unknown.  
The “Convention concerning the exchange of Greek and Turkish population" was signed at Lausanne, on 30 January 1923, by the two governments. It involved approximately 2 million people (around 1.5 million Anatolian and 500,000 Muslims in Greece), most of whom were forcibly made refugees.

5213376b-6aff-55de-afcc-32cf7bfb66d1.name: Portrait of Paul Draneht
5213376b-6aff-55de-afcc-32cf7bfb66d1.author: Massimiliano Cremona, Ignazio Galella
5213376b-6aff-55de-afcc-32cf7bfb66d1.second_name: Paul Draneht (1815–1894), the Superintendent of the Cairo Opera who commissioned Aida from Giuseppe Verdi
5213376b-6aff-55de-afcc-32cf7bfb66d1.description2:
Paul Draneht (1815-1894) was born in Nicosia (Cyprus) as Pavlos Pavlidis. He was the child of a Greek Christian Orthodox family who fled Cyprus due to the clashes between Greeks and Turks, and took refuge in Egypt. Muhammad (Mehmet) Ali Pasha (the Khedive of Egypt) sent him to study in France. Trusted by the Khedive (who awarded him the titles of Bey and Pasha), Paul Draneht participated in the negotiations regarding the opening of the Suez Canal.  
He became superintendent of the Egyptian Opera Theatre and commissioned the opera Aida to the Italian composer Giuseppe Verdi. The Aida opened in Cairo on 24 December 1871.

521421e0-80f1-5225-89de-67bdaec30210.name: Narrow street in Pera, Istanbul
521421e0-80f1-5225-89de-67bdaec30210.author: Maria Dimitriadou
521421e0-80f1-5225-89de-67bdaec30210.description2: A black and white photo from a leather bound album. It bepicts a narrow street in Pera, Constantinople, leading to the church of “Panagia tou Stavrodromiou”. Photographer unknown.

523087c9-9a15-54a0-b37b-745c43c2cb51.name: An olive oil factory run by an Italian migrant in Monastir (Tunisia)
523087c9-9a15-54a0-b37b-745c43c2cb51.author: Giulia Barrera
523087c9-9a15-54a0-b37b-745c43c2cb51.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 217
523087c9-9a15-54a0-b37b-745c43c2cb51.description2: According to a 1895 survey by the Italian Chamber of Commerce of Tunisia, 82 modern olive-oil industries operated in the country; 34 (41 per cent) were run by Italians, 24 by French nationals, 19 by Tunisians and the remaining five by persons of other nationalities.

5296fe8d-c29c-5ac6-9be6-323c7b48cdf1.name: Fleeing the barbarians on the road to Amiens
5296fe8d-c29c-5ac6-9be6-323c7b48cdf1.keywords: Forced migration; exodus; First World War; France
5296fe8d-c29c-5ac6-9be6-323c7b48cdf1.description2: Around 700,000 French citizens fled the country in the face of the German invasion at the beginning of the First World War (Spring 1914–1915). Pictured here are families who have abandoned their homes in a  hurry, taking just a few belongings with them on these carts.
