e80dfa93-78f5-57ec-a258-0a31de9fef63.name: *The daughter of the English ambassador riding in a palanquin*
e80dfa93-78f5-57ec-a258-0a31de9fef63.archival: Orientalist Paintings Collection-Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation Collection
e80dfa93-78f5-57ec-a258-0a31de9fef63.keywords: Fausto Zonaro; Guillemet; Orientalism; painting; İstanbul
e80dfa93-78f5-57ec-a258-0a31de9fef63.description2: Until he was appointed as the court painter in 1896, Zonaro was predominantly commissioned by European embassies in Istanbul. In his memoirs, the artist reveals that British Ambassador Sir Philip William Currie (1894-96), who was one of Zonaro’s clients, commissioned a painting depicting his stepdaughter on the palanquin on her way to the church to marry a diplomat. Sir Currie also requested the view of the Golden Horn – as seen from the garden of the embassy – to be included in the background of the painting. The palanquin carriers, two embassy officials smartly dressed in their uniforms and the young woman sitting on the palanquin in her bridal veil, posed for the artist for several days.

e826dd7d-b40a-53fb-88ca-e2af297d1f40.name: Jacket

e87a28c8-480d-590e-ba3c-b84ef6e8d476.name: Abdul-Mejid I, Sultan of Turkey (1823–1861)
e87a28c8-480d-590e-ba3c-b84ef6e8d476.keywords: Abdul-Mejid, Sultan of Turkey; Egypt; Syria, Palestine; Hungarian refugees
e87a28c8-480d-590e-ba3c-b84ef6e8d476.description2: Portrait of Abdul-Mejid I, Sultan of Turkey (1823–1861), riding a horse. When he came to power in 1839, he tried to re-occupy lands lost to Muhammad 'Ali Pasha, the ruler of Egypt. In this effort he was supported by Britain and Austria. In 1840 a combined British-Austrian fleet cut off the supply lines of the Egyptian army and forced the Egyptians to sign the 1840 Convention of Alexandria. Abdul-Mejid was able to win back Syria and Palestine. In 1849 he granted the Hungarian refugees exile. In 1861 he died and left his throne to his brother Abdülaziz.

e8867b07-6d42-5182-8664-51768b182008.name: Abd al-Kader at Amboise
e8867b07-6d42-5182-8664-51768b182008.description2: Emir 'Abd al-Kader was the symbol of Algerian resistance to the French occupation from 1832 to 1847. After his resignation in 1847, he was taken to the Château de Pau, followed by hundreds of people, where he was detained until he was moved to the Château d'Amboise. His behaviour during his time in captivity attracted the admiration of the French, who saw him as a romantic hero: he studied, meditated, and was always ready to receive visitors. The various portraits and photographs of him that were produced portrayed him as a pious man rather than the warrior he had been. In 1852, the Prince Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte went to Amboise to officially announce the end of his captivity.

e952d626-e57d-5b8e-b2e2-24763b1c7b83.name: Receipt for a subscription among the Italians in Tunisia to buy Italy a plane
e952d626-e57d-5b8e-b2e2-24763b1c7b83.author: Massimo Sanacore
e952d626-e57d-5b8e-b2e2-24763b1c7b83.archival: ASLi, Famiglia Moreno di Tunisi, b. 6
e952d626-e57d-5b8e-b2e2-24763b1c7b83.description2:
We do not know whether the Italians living in Tunisia who collected money to buy Italy a plane were aware that Italy would use planes to bomb civilians in Libya. To be sure, they supported Italian expansionist policy.  
This receipt bears the signature of the treasurer of the committee that was collecting funding to buy Italy a plane, Giuseppe Di Vittorio, the owner of a successful construction company. The donor, Ugo Moreno, was another “big man” of the Italian community in Tunisia: a lawyer, he established a bank (Banca Italiana di Credito), in 1901 started an oil company (Societé du Pétrole) and in 1919 became town councillor in Tunis.

en: Sanacore, Massimo, "Storia della famiglia di Moisè Moreno", *Nuovi studi livornesi*, 18 (2011): 347–53.

e97ad326-57ea-571c-be97-f63b11fcafbc.name: Chorographical plan of the attack waged by Lord Exmouth against Algiers on 27 August 1816
e97ad326-57ea-571c-be97-f63b11fcafbc.author: Edoardo Garis, Giulia Barrera
e97ad326-57ea-571c-be97-f63b11fcafbc.archival: ASTo, Carte Topografiche e disegni, Carte Topografiche Segrete, Algeri 3 E I Rosso (1816)
e97ad326-57ea-571c-be97-f63b11fcafbc.third_name: *Plan / de l'attaque donnée à Alger / par S.E. Lord Exmouth / le 27. Août 1816. / et levé sur le lieu même par un Ingénieur / de la Flotte Anglaise / publié à Turin en décembre 1816. / Avec permission et privilege du Roi*
e97ad326-57ea-571c-be97-f63b11fcafbc.description2: In the spring 1816, a large Anglo-Dutch fleet headed by Admiral Lord Exmouth forced the three Ottoman regencies of the so-called “Barbary Coast” (the coastline of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli; “Barbary” comes from “Berber”, the name given to the original people and culture of North-West Africa) to release Christian captives and to sign agreements over the abolition of corsairing, or privateering, and the enslavement of captives. In August, the Anglo-Dutch fleet returned to Algiers and made additional demands to the Turkish regent, who refused to comply. Lord Exmouth then ordered a heavy bombardment that destroyed the Algerian navy and part of the city of Algiers.

en: Clancy-Smith, Julia, *Mediterraneans: North Africa and Europe in an Age of Migration, c. 1800–1900*, Oakland, CA: University of California Press, 2011.

ea69f41d-1b91-5ee4-8097-8aba9db33c0f.name: *Le consul Joseph Raffo* (painting)
ea69f41d-1b91-5ee4-8097-8aba9db33c0f.holder: Musée d’Histoire Moderne et Contemporaine de Kassar Saïd
ea69f41d-1b91-5ee4-8097-8aba9db33c0f.author: Bechir Yazidi
ea69f41d-1b91-5ee4-8097-8aba9db33c0f.materials: Canvas, wood, coloured pigments, gold leaf
ea69f41d-1b91-5ee4-8097-8aba9db33c0f.description2: Giuseppe Maria Joseph Raffo, the subject of this painting, was born in Tunis in 1795 and is depicted here in full uniform with the air of an important Turkish dignitary. He entered service as a secretary to Bey Hassine, and later served as Tunisia's Minister for Foreign Affairs under his rule as well as that of his successors, despite being a Sardinian subject all the while. He made a fortune by taking over a tuna farm in the Cap Bon region in the form of private concession. This painting is evidence of an active diplomatic relationship between the Palais du Bardo and the European chancelleries.

ead4767a-7d82-5048-a0d2-07b5b5b4d68a.name: Table of of Krste Petkov Misirkov
ead4767a-7d82-5048-a0d2-07b5b5b4d68a.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
ead4767a-7d82-5048-a0d2-07b5b5b4d68a.description2: Krste Petkov Misirkov (1874–1926) was actively engaged in politics, fighting for the recognition of Macedonians as a people with distinct tradition and language. He is one of the few who made great contribution to raising international awareness of Macedonian people at the close of the 19th century and in the early 20th century.

eca99cf6-1929-5d7d-bf2a-e8ec044b0d68.name: A Jewish family
eca99cf6-1929-5d7d-bf2a-e8ec044b0d68.description2: The Jewish community, which had gone through various waves of migration since the beginning of the Islamic period, had, by the 19th century, become an important part of Tunisian society.

ee0cbe27-f7a7-56db-b5c5-18038a38b0c8.name: Omar Pasha (1806–1871)
ee0cbe27-f7a7-56db-b5c5-18038a38b0c8.keywords: Omar Pasha; Croatia; Bosnia; Ottoman empire; Herzegovina
ee0cbe27-f7a7-56db-b5c5-18038a38b0c8.description2: Portrait of Omar Pasha. He was born in Croatia in 1806 near the Turkish-Hungarian border. In 1828 he deserted from the Austrian army and joined the Ottoman administration in Bosnia. After a long career in the Ottoman army, he became the military governor of Bucharest and commanded the Ottoman forces at the siege of Sevastopol in Crimea. In 1862 he suppressed an uprising in Herzogovina and led a victorious campaign against Montenegro. In 1868 he became War Minister and died in 1871 in Istanbul.

efb40382-898f-59c5-99c9-337e5b9fd997.name: Europeans leaving Alexandria (Egypt) during the antiforeign rioting in June 1882
efb40382-898f-59c5-99c9-337e5b9fd997.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
efb40382-898f-59c5-99c9-337e5b9fd997.author: Giulia Barrera
efb40382-898f-59c5-99c9-337e5b9fd997.third_name: *La partenza degli europei da Alessandria d’Egitto (da uno schizzo preso dal vero)*
efb40382-898f-59c5-99c9-337e5b9fd997.description2:
Ahmed Urabi, an army colonel of peasant origins, led a protest movement in 1881 against European domination of Egypt’s affairs and in favour of placing constitutional limits on the Khedive’s power. In 1882 Urabi was appointed minister of war and started working for the creation of a national assembly.  
In May 1882, Britain and France, concerned about access to the Suez Canal and intending to protect their financial interests in Egypt, sent a fleet to Alexandria, hoping to weaken Urabi’s nationalist movement. The presence of the fleet only worsened tensions. In June, anti-foreign rioting erupted in Alexandria and left several hundreds dead, including about 50 foreigners.  
18,665 Italians were living in Egypt at the time, mostly in Alexandria and Cairo.
efb40382-898f-59c5-99c9-337e5b9fd997.holding_institution_org: Biblioteca di Storia Moderna e Contemporanea

f23c34bf-814d-5e9e-8baf-ebe84ce157b4.name: *Folies Rambuteau. New quartet from the Auvergne.*
f23c34bf-814d-5e9e-8baf-ebe84ce157b4.description2: The 19th century saw mass rural to urban migration, particularly to Paris, for largely economic reasons. These migrants often settled with people from their region, who offered them work in specific fields. Thus, those from the Savoy region became specialised in chimney-sweeping, those from the Auvergne were water-carriers or coal-merchants, those from Brittany were domestic workers, and so on. Regional solidarity therefore ensured the survival of regional culture. In this image, for example, a quartet from the Auvergne are advertising their performance in a *café-concert* in traditional dress. Music from the Auvergne was the origin of the Parisian *bal-musette* (a dance accompanied by accordion music).

f29f00e9-279d-593b-8b54-54ee9c2bb477.name: Document on slavery
f29f00e9-279d-593b-8b54-54ee9c2bb477.holder: Palais de la Rose – Musée de l’Armée
f29f00e9-279d-593b-8b54-54ee9c2bb477.author: Bechir Yazidi

f29f00e9-279d-593b-8b54-54ee9c2bb477.description2: This document is written in English on two sheets of parchment. Source: United States of America. Length: 30 cm. Width: 40 cm.

f4c22e70-95b9-576e-af85-4267539e8ace.name: Précis Historique de la Traite des Noirs et de l'Esclavage Colonial
f4c22e70-95b9-576e-af85-4267539e8ace.description2: This illustration, taken from the Précis Historique de la Traite des Noirs et de l'Esclavage Colonial  had didactic objectives. It attempted to show the inhuman treatment slaves were subjected to (yoke, chains, whipping) by traders. In this image, a mother is begging King Charles X of France to spare her son this dark fate and abolish slavery. However, even though the National Convention did abolish slavery in 1794, Napoléon Bonaparte then reintroduced it to most of the territories under French control.

f4d69a3e-9925-5ec2-a00c-7db5ff29d9d2.name: Register listing 'all of the subjects of the Grand Duke of Tuscany [Italy] residing in Tunisia'
f4d69a3e-9925-5ec2-a00c-7db5ff29d9d2.author: Massimo Sanacore
f4d69a3e-9925-5ec2-a00c-7db5ff29d9d2.archival: ASLi, Governo civile e militare, b. 433
f4d69a3e-9925-5ec2-a00c-7db5ff29d9d2.third_name: *Stato nominativo di tutti i Sudditi di Sua Altezza Reale il Gran Duca di Toscana residenti in Tunisi*
f4d69a3e-9925-5ec2-a00c-7db5ff29d9d2.description2:
The names appearing in this list are mostly Jewish, including that of Giacomo Castelnuovo (Livorno, Italy, 1819 – La Goulette, Tunisia, 1886), a medical doctor who had to flee Italy because of his liberal ideas and his support for Italy’s national unification. Initially he went to Egypt, where he founded two Italian newspapers, *Lo Spettatore Egiziano* and *Il Progresso d’Egitto*.  
The author of many medical publications, in Tunis Castelnuovo became the Bey’s personal physician. He served as president of the Tunisian branch of the Alliance Israélite Universelle, and promoted the construction of a synagogue, on a plot of land granted by the Bey.  
A Freemason, he fought in Italy in the wars for Italy’s unification. He was awarded honours by both the Italian King (who ennobled him) and by the Bey of Tunis.

f4ee2a86-2553-5a0f-a698-a195e71a3ffd.name: Treaty of the French Protectorate, 12 May 1881
f4ee2a86-2553-5a0f-a698-a195e71a3ffd.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
f4ee2a86-2553-5a0f-a698-a195e71a3ffd.author: Bechir Yazidi
f4ee2a86-2553-5a0f-a698-a195e71a3ffd.keywords: French protectorate in Tunisia; Sadok Pacha Bey; General Bréart
f4ee2a86-2553-5a0f-a698-a195e71a3ffd.description2: This drawing shows an important moment in modern Tunisian history: the signing of the treaty of the French Protectorate over the Tunisian regency, at the Palais Kassar Saïd, in Bardo, on 12 May 1881. The main players are featured in this drawing, namely Sadok Bey who ruled Tunisia from 1859 to 1882, with his hand resting on the table, and to his right the general Jules Aimé Bréart, the leader of the invading French troops.

f596dba8-2ee8-5042-9e06-4a090887dd12.name: Armchair of Krste Petkov Misirkov
f596dba8-2ee8-5042-9e06-4a090887dd12.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
f596dba8-2ee8-5042-9e06-4a090887dd12.description2: Krste Petkov Misirkov (1874–1926) was an imposing figure that contributed to the standardization of the modern Macedonian language. He lived and worked in St. Petersburg, Russia. Misirkov’s book “On Macedonian Matters” is a starting point in explaining Macedonian distinctiveness, having served as an intellectual and contemplative engine for generations of Macedonians fighting in the battlefield and in literature alike.

f62eb2d5-765a-5d02-9c15-324361c4a2e6.name: *The Mansion of Alexandros Lukas Benakis in Alexandria*
f62eb2d5-765a-5d02-9c15-324361c4a2e6.author: Maria Dimitriadou
f62eb2d5-765a-5d02-9c15-324361c4a2e6.description2: Black and white photos on a family album depicting the mansion of Alexander Lucas Benakis near Alexandria. Photographer unknown.

f6a973df-a6b0-51b8-8bb0-fd4026b06319.name: Photograph of Ion Ghica (sitting)
f6a973df-a6b0-51b8-8bb0-fd4026b06319.description2: In 1848, Ion Ghica was the envoy of the Wallachian revolutionaries to Istanbul, where he remained after the suppression of the revolution. He created connections among the Ottoman officials, being appreciated by Reshid-Pasha (Grand Vizier from 1854), and became a supporter of the Romanian Principalities’ union under Ottoman sovereignty. A former journalist, he devised the project (not realized) for an economic and literary periodical, published in all the languages spoken in the Empire. In 1854 he was appointed governor of the island of Samos, where he took measures against piracy and founded several schools (a middle school, an agricultural school, a marine school and a girls’ institute). His activity earned him the title of “prince”(bey) of Samos, which he received from sultan Abdülmecid in February 1856.

f94fb43c-ce0a-57b2-b9cb-171b27871fa2.name: *Arabs of the Desert*
f94fb43c-ce0a-57b2-b9cb-171b27871fa2.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
f94fb43c-ce0a-57b2-b9cb-171b27871fa2.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
f94fb43c-ce0a-57b2-b9cb-171b27871fa2.description2: The constant movement of large Bedouin confederations regularly impacted on the history of the Middle East, in particular when it affected settled societies and cities.This print provides much interesting detail about the dress of the Bedouin at the time David Roberts visited the Near East in 1838/9. The individual in the foreground wears a white turban and short gown with belt, a dark red jacket and a voluminous, all-enveloping blue cloak. His legs remain uncovered, and he wears simple leather sandals on his feet. A formidable dagger or khanjar in its sheath is secured in his belt, and he carries a long slender gun through a sling. The bullets for the gun appear to be secured in an ammunition belt strapped diagonally across his chest. In the background, four male figures wearing striped headscarfs and cloaks as well as short white gowns and holdings lances appear on the right. On the left, a bedouin leads his camels away. The inscription states: *Arabs of the tribe of Benisaid, Feb. 17th 1839*.
f94fb43c-ce0a-57b2-b9cb-171b27871fa2.artist_birthplace: David Roberts: Edinburgh, Scotland; Louis Hague: Tournai, Belgium

f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.name: Yemeni dagger
f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.author: Huda Kilani
f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.keywords: double edged blade; hilts; geometric designs; silver filigree; suspension rings; arms; armours; metalwork; fashion; accessories
f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.description2: A dagger with a double-edged blade, an oblong-head hilt and silver filigree work in geometric designs; it is carried on a woollen belt with leather strap-work, usually with six asymmetrical suspension rings. Yemeni and Hijazi daggers have different shapes and their diffusion on the territory of Jordan shows how population movements, trade and exchange were common in the area.

fb62d82c-bb0f-5b66-b3bd-e65d7480fe70.name: *Suqs*
fb62d82c-bb0f-5b66-b3bd-e65d7480fe70.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
fb62d82c-bb0f-5b66-b3bd-e65d7480fe70.history:
The *suqs* of the Tunis medina, particularly those specialising by trade, play an important economic role in the city. Some examples are:  
  
• Suq el-Chaouchiya (selling chechias, woollen hats). Founded by the community of Muslims who had been expelled from Spain in the 17th century.  
• Suq Ettrouk (Turkish *suq*)  
• Suq el-Attarine (selling perfume).  
• Suq el-Nahas (selling brass and copper).  
• Suq el-Bey, founded by Hammouda Pacha (1781–1813)  
  
Located near the Zaytuna Mosque, these are the best *suqs* in the Tunis medina. The chechia industry particularly was at its peak here in the 19th century. Today, despite the undeniable decrease in demand, chechia production has survived by adapting to a new clientele, and has become the most popular artisanal Tunisian product with tourists.
fb62d82c-bb0f-5b66-b3bd-e65d7480fe70.description2: The *suqs* have preserved their beautiful architecture to this day, with different columns, pointed arches, and dark, cool rooms lit by the natural light streaming in through the holes in the whitewashed, vaulted ceilings. Located by the great Zaytuna Mosque, these *suqs* are always busy and full of life. Each *suq* is composed of a large central street, with a number of small shops and workshops opening up onto neighbouring narrower alleys, which are covered with vaulted ceilings, made with bricks arranged in different ways to form endless geometric patterns. The woodwork on the shops and their hobnailed doors, painted in a thousand colours and decorated with calligraphic designs, add to the *suq*'s spectacular appearance.

fc5492b4-b79e-5ab6-acf3-8e4d44f66cbc.name: The villa of Paul Draneht in Oggebbio (Verbania, Italy)
fc5492b4-b79e-5ab6-acf3-8e4d44f66cbc.author: Massimiliano Cremona, Ignazio Galella
fc5492b4-b79e-5ab6-acf3-8e4d44f66cbc.archival: Intra: Tipografia Intrese, no date (but postal stamp of 1906)
fc5492b4-b79e-5ab6-acf3-8e4d44f66cbc.description2:
In 1872, Paul Draneht Bey bought a Villa on the Lago Maggiore (Italy), which he remodelled, mixing oriental and European architectural styles. From this postcard, one can see a tower with an Arabic flavour.  
In the interior, there was an “Egyptian hall”, modelled according to the style of an ancient Upper-Egypt temple. The furniture was made by one of the shops in Paris that was making the scenes for the opera *Aida*.

fc6ac8e2-2fed-5243-b1e6-1e00ea0b5928.name: Hôpital Charles Nicolle
fc6ac8e2-2fed-5243-b1e6-1e00ea0b5928.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
fc6ac8e2-2fed-5243-b1e6-1e00ea0b5928.history: The first great hospital to be built following the establishment of the protectorate, the Hôpital Charles Nicolle initially accepted only French patients. Having been established initially by a beylical decree on 9 June 1897, it was renamed after the doctor Charles Nicolle, the director of l'Institut Pasteur in Tunis from 1903 to 1936 and 1928 Nobel Prize for Physiology winner, in 1944. The Hôpital Charles Nicolle became known for its pioneering work and specialism in virologic diagnosis, congenital illnesses and paediatric nephrology.
fc6ac8e2-2fed-5243-b1e6-1e00ea0b5928.keywords: Charles Nicolle; Institut Pasteur; Nobel prize
fc6ac8e2-2fed-5243-b1e6-1e00ea0b5928.description2: This hospital was built over 12 hectares, at the foot of the Rabta Hill just outside the ramparts of the city. It was designed by the architect Resplandy, with the help of Dr Bastide. The hospital initially provided two different kinds of general medicine services and surgery, and had 190 beds. Two more buildings were added during the 20th century. Today, the Hôpital Charles Nicolle is a renowned university hospital.

fd211c5e-6b0a-584a-8a00-0307908a3402.name: Request for financial help to the Minister of the Interior by Filippo Codispoti, a former Italian migrant to Cairo, who had to flee Egypt with his family in 1882
fd211c5e-6b0a-584a-8a00-0307908a3402.author: Fortunata Chindemi, Maria Fortunata Minasi
fd211c5e-6b0a-584a-8a00-0307908a3402.archival: ASRC, Prefettura di Gabinetto, inv.34 b.212 fasc.8118
fd211c5e-6b0a-584a-8a00-0307908a3402.description2:
In this letter Filippo Codispoti explained to the Italian Minister of Interior that he was born in Reggio Calabria (a town in Southern Italy) and was 17 years old before he migrated to Egypt. After years of hard work he had been able to reach a comfortable position and was running a wine and liquor shop, while his son was working as a shoemaker, and his daily pay was five and a half lire.  
He further explained that the civil war in Egypt had forced him to flee the country together with his wife and three children, leaving all his belongings in Egypt. He was now penniless and reduced to utter misery, and asked the government for financial help.  
According to governmental statistics, in 1882 there were 18,665 Italians in Egypt. The number of foreigners in Egypt totalled 90,886.
fd211c5e-6b0a-584a-8a00-0307908a3402.holding_institution_org: Archivio di Stato di Reggio Calabria

fdf4838a-7764-5f27-afc8-32377c84dfbc.name: *The interior of Mustapha Pacha's palace*
fdf4838a-7764-5f27-afc8-32377c84dfbc.author: Dalila Orfali
fdf4838a-7764-5f27-afc8-32377c84dfbc.description2: In the early 19th century this palace, located in the Algiers kasbah, housed the collections of the first library museum. It was also the home of one of the regency's most famous deys, Mustapha Pacha, who ordered many of the old town's monuments to be built during his reign. One example of these is the great palace of Menzel el-Mahalla in east Algiers, which was later partly destroyed, with the rest being used as a hospital for the French expeditionary corps. The dey was assassinated in 1805.

fe6cec92-b619-55f4-a18b-3a0f8fd470af.name: Palais-Musée du Bardo
fe6cec92-b619-55f4-a18b-3a0f8fd470af.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
fe6cec92-b619-55f4-a18b-3a0f8fd470af.history: The museum occupies just a part of the entire Palais du Bardo, a collection of buildings constructed from the early 15th century onwards. It was built in the style of Andalusian princely residences, but also shows traces of North African Tunisian and Italian architectural influences dating to the Husainid period when it underwent a series of modifications. The museum was opened and received its first archaeological collections on 7 May 1888 by the Bey of Tunisia and the French Resident-General. It remains, to this day, one of the most important archaeological museums in the world, and is particularly renowned for its excellent collection of Roman mosaics.
fe6cec92-b619-55f4-a18b-3a0f8fd470af.keywords: Architecture; art; painting; stucco; mosaic; marble; ceramics
fe6cec92-b619-55f4-a18b-3a0f8fd470af.description2: The Musée du Bardo receives more than 500,000 visitors each year. It is divided into three floors, each holding thousands of exceptionally valuable items, all of which tell the story of a country at the crossroads of multiple civilisations. Visitors can admire mosaics on the floors and walls, the statues, funerary steles, ceramics, jewellery, works of art and bronze and marble sculptures, ranging from the prehistoric era to Punic, Roman and Byzantine times.

fe898d65-6a28-56fc-93fb-7e1ee70f830f.name: *A landscape of Bazaar from Istanbul*
fe898d65-6a28-56fc-93fb-7e1ee70f830f.holder: Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University, Painting and Sculpture Museum
fe898d65-6a28-56fc-93fb-7e1ee70f830f.description2: At the beginning of the 19th century, romantic painters who appreciated eastern mysticism brought newly discovered eastern landscapes with their paintings which contained fiery colours and interesting landscapes. One of those painters coming to Istanbul from Malta and affected by eastern mysticism was Amadeo Preziosi. He usually painted scenes from daily life, such as shops between streets, coffeehouses, baths, peddlers passing the street, a woman filling water from a fountain and figures from different ethnic groups. Like many of his contemporaries, Preziosi had been lured to the exotic city of Istanbul. He also tried to reflect the cultural diversity of the city in his paintings. Especially in his watercolour paintings he loved expressing the blue water of the Bosporus with its caïques, pavilions, palaces, boats, mansions, residences, bazaars and cemeteries.

ff6c9c68-5a72-5102-ad19-99345287b4be.name: Letter from Marshall Forteguerri, commander general of the navy of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, confirming the purchase of Tunisian slaves in Naples
ff6c9c68-5a72-5102-ad19-99345287b4be.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
ff6c9c68-5a72-5102-ad19-99345287b4be.description2: This letter from Marshall Forteguerri, commander general of the navy of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, confirms the purchase of Tunisian slaves in Naples and their subsequent emancipation.
